editorialSections.title: ABA 512 turned "govern your AI" into a conduct duty

blocks.text: ABA Formal Opinion 512 reads the existing Model Rules onto generative AI: the duty of competent, confidential, candid, and supervised use already applies. The hard part is showing it. A firm that uses AI well but writes none of it down cannot demonstrate the practice when it counts. This scorecard checks for the documented controls that turn good intentions into a defensible record.
What it checks

Whether the controls each duty implies actually exist in writing: a policy every timekeeper acknowledged, a required human verification step, tool vetting for client confidentiality, named supervisory accountability, and a documentation trail.
What it can't do

It cannot tell you whether your firm is compliant, and it does not give legal advice. It maps your answers to published guidance and shows where your documented practice is thin. A licensed attorney interprets what that means for your obligations.

editorialSections.title: The most common mistake is building too much

blocks.text: Teams hear "AI" and picture a chatbot trained on their files. Often the real problem is that nobody can find last quarter's contract, and a naming convention plus a shared drive would fix it for a weekend of effort. The wrong system costs money, stalls, and gets abandoned. This checker walks down a ladder from the cheapest fix to the most involved one and stops at the first rung that meets your actual need.
What it does

Takes your answers about volume, formats, change rate, access, sensitivity, and what you need to do with the documents, then points to one primary recommendation with runner-ups, a plain-English rationale, and a first-week checklist.
What it will not do

It will not sell you the expensive option by default, and it does not give legal, security, or financial advice. It maps your inputs to a sensible starting point. A short conversation confirms whether that starting point is right for your specifics.

editorialSections.title: A ladder from cheapest fix to most involved

blocks.text: The checker weighs your answers and stops at the first rung that meets your real need. Higher rungs are more capable and more costly to build and maintain. The goal is the lowest rung that solves your problem, not the highest one you could imagine.
Organize folders + naming
A clean folder structure and a naming convention on the drive you already pay for. Cheapest, fastest, and enough for most small, stable document sets.
Write SOPs first
When the pain is a repeatable process rather than the files, a few written procedures beat any tool. Often the right first move before you build anything.
Notion or a doc hub
A shared workspace with pages, light structure, and search. Good when a handful of people need one place for living documents and notes.
Airtable or a database
When your records are consistent fields (clients, cases, inventory), a structured database beats documents. Filter, sort, and relate instead of hunting.
RAG / AI retrieval
When you need to ask questions across a large, changing pile of documents, AI retrieval reads them and answers with citations. Powerful, and the most setup.
Custom application
A purpose-built app when off-the-shelf tools truly cannot fit the workflow. The most capable and the most expensive; earn your way here.

editorialSections.title: "Just hire an AI consultant" is the confident wrong answer.
editorialSections.eyebrow: The Operator Execution Gap · practice build

blocks.text: The generic advice for standing up a practice is fluent and reassuring, and it skips the parts that actually determine whether the build survives its first year. Same question, two answers. The distance between them is the cost of a stalled build.
✕ Generic advice · ungrounded
"How do we build our own AI-consulting practice?"
"Hire an AI consultant or take a course, pick a few tools, and start offering services. Your domain expertise is the hard part — the rest is easy once you have someone who knows AI."

Confident. Fluent. Wrong about where practices actually fail. Tooling and a hire don't produce a practice; delivery infrastructure, a real pipeline, priced offers, and utilized capacity do. This advice sends you into a stalled build.
✓ Aloha AI · operations-grounded PS operating fundamentals
Same question, answered from how practices actually run:

A practice is an operating system, not a skill. The binding constraints are rarely AI knowledge. They are: a productized, priced offer you can sell repeatably; delivery infrastructure (scoping, QA, handoff) so quality doesn't depend on one person; a client pipeline matched to your delivery capacity; and utilization in the healthy band (roughly 70–90% billable, by firm type) that leaves room to sell and improve.

Miss the match between pipeline and capacity and you get one of two failure modes: bench risk (capacity idle, no demand) or delivery risk (sold more than you can deliver). Both stall the build. A hire fixes neither on its own.

Confidence: High Why you can rely on it: it maps to documented professional-services operating fundamentals (utilization/capacity, pipeline-to-headcount matching, and productization) cited in the method ledger below.
OEG (the Operator Execution Gap) is the distance between what generic advice says and what an organization can actually build and run. Closing it is the entire job.

editorialSections.title: A working AI habit and a mature AI workflow are two different things

blocks.text: Plenty of teams get good output from AI. Far fewer can say where the facts came from, who checked them, what data went into which tool, and whether the next person could run the same process and get the same quality. That gap is where risk lives. This audit checks the parts of an AI workflow that make it repeatable, verifiable, and defensible, so a good result stops depending on who happened to run it.
What it checks

Whether your workflow grounds output in real sources, gates it behind human review, protects confidential data, runs the same way every time, has documented ownership, and gets measured so it improves.
What it can't do

It cannot tell you whether your organization is compliant, and it does not give legal advice. It maps your answers to workflow-maturity practice and shows where the process is thin. A qualified advisor interprets what that means for your obligations.

Sources & grounding
Whether AI output is tied to real, checkable sources rather than the model's unaided guess.
Verification & QA
Whether a human reviews output and checks for hallucination before anything client-facing goes out.
Privacy & confidentiality
Whether there are rules about what data goes into which tools, and whether they are followed.
Handoff & reproducibility
Whether the workflow is a documented, repeatable process or an ad-hoc effort that lives in one head.
Governance & policy
Whether AI use is documented, owned, and accountable rather than assumed.
Measurement & improvement
Whether you track how the workflow performs and use what you learn to improve it.
